newsitem.title: Vietnam: Japan's Hashimoto, seeking ASEAN ties, to Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto, seeking ASEAN ties, to Vietnam.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto brought his bid for closer links with Southeast Asia to Vietnam on Saturday on the fourth stage of a five-nation trip which has been overshadowed by the hostage crisis in Peru.

Hanoi rolled out the red carpet for the state leader of its biggest aid donor and trading partner, while the communist country's official news agency reeled out reports peppered with the words "friendship" and "cooperation".
Hashimoto was greeted by Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, who expressed his government's concern about the 25-day-old hostage crisis inside the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, Peru.
He replied that Tokyo would continue to place its faith in the Peruvian government, which has renewed talks with Marxist rebels to secure the release of the 74 remaining hostages.
On his arrival, Hashimoto signed a stack of new aid agreements for Vietnam worth some $765 million -- mostly loans to improve the poverty-hit country's creaking infrastructure.

Japan is by far and away the leading donor of official development aid to poverty-hit Vietnam, pledging $3.23 billion between 1992 and 1996. Of the record $2.4 billion committed by donors for this year, its share is about one third.

Japanese Foreign Ministry Spokesman Ken Shimanouchi told reporters after the prime ministers' meeting that Japan would continue to support Hanoi's decade-old drive to reform its economy along market lines.

He said Hashimoto had urged Kiet to improve the environment for foreign investors in Vietnam, where Japanese companies are ranked second in a long list of countries seeking a share in the booming economy.

However, he stressed his desire to broaden relations beyond the economic sphere -- a message he had already taken to Brunei, Malaysia and Indonesia and is to repeat in a key policy speech in Singapore next Tuesday.
All five countries are members of the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which Vietnam joined in 1995.
Hashimoto's vision of greater solidarity embraced cooperation on regional security, though Simanouchi denied that was a move to build a strategic alliance as a balance against China.

"This visit was about enhancing Japan's ties with ASEAN," he said. "We believe that this will be conducive to creating peace and stability in the entire Asia-Pacific region, and it will benefit everybody in the region."
He said Hashimoto had invited Vietnam's foreign minister to visit Japan and, calling for enhanced security dialogue, renewed an invitation for its deputy defence minister to visit too.
Hashimoto, who marked his first anniversary in office on Saturday, also paid a courtesy visit to Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi.
On Sunday he is due to visit the mausoleum of Ho Chi Minh, the revered founding father of modern-day Vietnam, before leaving for Singapore.
